title: One cell, ten hours
hook: A bacterium splits every 20 minutes. How crowded is the dish after 10 hours?

knows: bacteria multiply by splitting in two
doesNotKnow: that a closed dish stops growth by running out of food

misconception: Growth feels steady, so 10 hours is about 10 times one hour of growth, and it can go on forever.
objective: The learner can explain that 10 hours of 20-minute doublings is 30 doublings, about a billion cells, that most of that growth happens at the very end, and that a finite food supply bends the curve and stops it.

claims.text: One cell doubling 30 times (10 hours of 20-minute doublings) gives 2^30 = 1,073,741,824 cells, about 1.07 billion.
At 7 hours the colony was 2.1 million cells, under 1% of its 10-hour size; at 9 h 40 min it was 537 million, half the 10-hour size, so half of all cells arrived in the last 20 minutes.
claims.source: At 7 h (21 doublings) 2^21 = 2,097,152 = 0.2% of 2^30. At 9 h 40 min (29 doublings) 2^29 = 536,870,912 = exactly half of 2^30.

claims.text: With one batch of food, growth looks the same at first, then bends and levels off near 100 million cells (91.5 million at 10 hours) as the food runs out.
claims.source: Stage model (convention): logistic growth N(k) = K / (1 + (K - 1) e^(-k ln 2)) per 20-minute step with K = 100 million. Gives 512 cells at 3 h (same as unlimited), 57 million at 9 h and 91 million at 10 h, approaching but never exceeding 100 million.

claims.text: In a closed culture, growth slows and stops when nutrients run out (or waste builds up); unlimited doubling cannot continue.
claims.source: Monod, J. (1949), 'The growth of bacterial cultures', Annual Review of Microbiology 3: 371-394; Madigan et al., Brock Biology of Microorganisms, chapter on microbial growth (batch culture growth curve).

claims.text: E. coli can double about every 20 minutes in rich lab broth; many bacteria, and E. coli in poorer conditions, divide far more slowly.
claims.source: Madigan et al., Brock Biology of Microorganisms (generation times); Sezonov, Joseleau-Petit & D'Ari (2007), 'Escherichia coli physiology in Luria-Bertani broth', Journal of Bacteriology 189(23): 8746-8749.

claims.text: The drawing is scaled: colony area is proportional to the number of cells, and 2^30 cells fill the dish (the stage calls this 100%). The 100-million food batch is made up.
claims.source: Modelling and drawing choice in Demo.tsx (FULL = 2^30, K = 1e8).

recall.question: Yeast with plenty of food doubles every 2 hours. Starting from 1,000 cells, about how many are there after one day?
recall.why: 24 hours is 12 doublings, and 2^12 = 4,096, so 1,000 cells become about 4.1 million, as long as the food lasts.
